section.title: Senior scope grows in depth, breadth, and time horizon
section.deck: Philip Su explains why the highest engineering levels require qualitative judgment and illustrates that scope through building Meta’s London engineering site.

blocks.question: What distinguishes the work at E7, E8, and E9?
answer: Philip Su begins with scope of influence: how large, valuable, or long-running an effort can someone reliably bring to completion? He offers approximate historical expectations, such as influencing roughly ten to fifteen people at senior/staff-adjacent levels and perhaps fifty at E7. He explicitly warns that his leveling information may be stale. These are illustrations from his experience, not a promotion standard for any company today.

Higher levels also differ qualitatively. An unusually deep specialist may solve problems that several less-senior engineers cannot substitute for. A broad generalist may integrate many kinds of work for a small or new team more effectively than separate hires. Headcount alone misses that distinction.

He recalls E9 being created after his initial E8 promotion and early decisions involving only a few very different candidates. Such a small and varied group makes a universal checklist implausible. At the top, informed judgment from peers and more-senior leaders matters: do they recognize work of that level, and why? He compares it to the qualitative recognition involved in academic seniority. The point is not that all evaluation is arbitrary, but that a list of tasks cannot fully represent exceptional and varied contributions.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: What if a strong E7 has no E8 or E9 nearby to learn from or assess them?
answer: Su recognizes the problem both in small companies and in weaker teams inside huge organizations. Being the strongest local person can distort self-calibration or remove opportunities to observe better judgment. He recommends an environment where there is room to grow alongside strong colleagues, rather than treating being locally best as the only goal.

At very high levels, merely copying another senior person may not work because their archetype and strengths can differ from yours. He favors access to a coach who participates in the relevant promotion decisions and can give a qualitative assessment. That person can explain where the work remains short of the bar and help discuss what stronger work would look like. The desired input is specific feedback, not an assumption that proximity to a prestigious title automatically produces growth.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.question: What scope of work contributed to your own E9 promotion?
answer: Su helped start Meta’s London engineering presence with twelve people and, over roughly four or five years, grow it to around four or five hundred. He describes managing the strategic and organizational transitions as the site expanded. A team of twelve could be run well by a capable engineering manager; several orders of magnitude of growth made problems more varied and answers less clear-cut.

One example was planning London internships and headcount based on anticipated visa constraints affecting future full-time arrivals in Menlo Park. He used data to recommend decisions roughly eighteen months before their consequences. Another was examining the site’s seniority distribution and whether engineers were developing at appropriate rates, rather than only checking each person’s nominal level.

The increased scope involved both breadth of people affected and the time horizon of judgment. He presents a collection of such decisions as the promotion story rather than naming one isolated code change or asserting that simply growing a site guarantees the same level.
blocks.speaker: Philip Su

blocks.title: Several ways for senior scope to grow
rows: Coordinate and influence a wider collection of people and decisions.
Solve qualitative technical problems that adding less-senior engineers cannot reproduce.
Combine many kinds of work where a strong generalist matters.
Use evidence now to choose actions whose effects arrive much later.
